prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The scientific case is a rare complete chain from basic hormone biology to a drug class: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36), receptor signalling, and then durable agonists whose efficacy has been replicated in many large randomized trials across diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The mechanism is stable and independently confirmed, and the clinical effect is large and still expanding, so recognition is neither premature nor contested on maturity. A prize to the physiological discoverers (Holst, Drucker) and the peptide-identification contribution (Mojsov) honours the discovery that made the drugs possible and keeps the configuration within three people.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for identifying the active peptide is disputed and other contributors outside the credited names may have comparable claims. Choosing three of four names leaves out Knudsen, whose acylated long-acting analogues are what actually reached patients, so the prize could be read as honouring the science while omitting the translation that produced the clinical impact. If the committee judges that the clinical transformation is the achievement, the trio is arguably incomplete or mis-weighted. I also cannot verify the detailed priority history from the supplied material.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the trio should cover discovery, mechanism and translation, and that Mojsov's claim is contested.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's analogue design is what delivered the clinical benefit, and I do not dismiss it. But this prize has historically honoured the discovery that opened the field, and the peptide-identification step is a scientific discovery, not an industrial optimisation. Contested priority argues for careful wording in the citation, not for removing the only credited person whose work is the identification of the active form. I would keep Mojsov, and if the committee prefers the translational emphasis I would want that argued explicitly as a change in what the prize rewards, not as a fix for an attribution dispute.

responses.point: El-Manira supported Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, noting that credit for peptide identification is contested and that Knudsen's work is largely industrial. He ranked UPR (B045) third and optogenetics second.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on the point that the contested peptide credit must be handled with a careful citation. I differ on optogenetics ranking above the UPR pair: with six credited names for at most three places and a real question whether it is a tool or a discovery, I find it harder to assign cleanly than Mori and Walter. I accept that its impact on circuit neuroscience is more extensive than I credited in my own ranking, but the allocation problem remains unresolved and I would not move it into my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (B031) second, as a clean two-person paradigm shift for chronic inflammatory disease with more than two decades of confirmation.
responses.response: I ranked TNF last on my own ballot and I want to qualify that fairly. The clinical impact and maturity are clear, and Feldmann and Maini form a clean pair. My reservation is that it reads more as translation of earlier cytokine biology than as a new discovery of principle, and your own uncertainty acknowledges this. I do not think it competes with GLP-1 on originality, but it is a serious candidate for a later year, and I would put it ahead of the HPV vaccines for that reason.

responses.point: Svenningsson placed the UPR (B045) second and CAR-T (B051) fourth, and questioned whether the clinical payoff of the UPR is sufficient and whether optogenetics, as a tool, fits the category.
responses.response: On the UPR I think the question about clinical payoff is the wrong test for a discovery of this kind. Walter and Mori defined a new signalling logic, and its conceptual reach into proteostasis and secretory disease stands on its own. Where I would press back is on ranking it above CAR-T: CAR-T has multiple approved products and durable remissions, but its attribution is incomplete without Eshhar, so I see the UPR as the cleaner configuration and CAR-T as the stronger clinical case. That difference is why I name both as alternatives and do not claim one dominates.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked TOR signalling (B001) third and argued that Hall is the clearest core, with the mammalian mTOR credit spread across several groups.
responses.response: I agree that Hall is the clear core and that Schreiber, Sabatini and others share a distributed, contested mammalian discovery. That is precisely why I think TOR is not ready as a three-person prize this year, and why I rank it behind the UPR and CAR-T. A smaller, Hall-centred configuration is defensible, but it risks leaving out groups whose contribution to the mammalian target is real, and I would want that credit analysis made explicit before supporting it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to honour the basic physiology and peptide identification or the translational drug development (Knudsen) as the core of the GLP-1 prize.
Priority for identification of the active GLP-1 peptide and the claims of contributors outside the credited names, which I cannot verify from the supplied material.
Whether the UPR or CAR-T is the stronger second option if the GLP-1 attribution cannot be settled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I have co-authored with committee colleague Sten Linnarsson and with Jonas Frisén, but neither is a credited name on the shortlist, and shared KI affiliation is not itself a conflict.
